summary:
Moonbase is an educational lunar-base survival game built by Team Qcold for NASA Space Apps 2026. The player runs a research station for 20 days. They place modules such as habitat, life support, solar panels and greenhouse. They manage oxygen, water, food, energy and crew health, and survive a life-support failure, a solar flare and the 14-day lunar night.

Real NASA data drives the game. The flare comes from the DONKI space-weather database, radiation figures from ISS RadLab, and facts from the OSDR archive appear in the end-of-mission debrief. The goal is to teach why real missions need shelters, power storage and local resources by letting players make those trade-offs themselves.

It is built with TypeScript, React 19, Vite and Node.js, on a deterministic game engine that also powers a co-op multiplayer mode over Server-Sent Events. Sound is generated entirely in code with the Web Audio API, and the game supports Ukrainian, English and Russian.
details:
Project details

What it does and how it works
Moonbase is an educational survival strategy game about running the first permanent research station on the Moon. The player leads a 20-day mission (90 seconds of real time per game day) on an isometric map. They place modules: habitat, life support, solar panels, batteries, greenhouse, radiation shelter, ice extractor, regolith quarry, storage and a medical bay. Four crew members (engineer, scientist, doctor, technician) build the base, get tasks, fall ill, and their morale reacts to how the mission goes. The player balances six resources: oxygen, water, food, energy, crew health and materials. Scripted hazards test the plan:

  • a life-support failure on day 6;
  • a solar flare on day 9;
  • builders falling ill;
  • the 14-day lunar night (days 14–20), when solar panels go dark and the base survives on stored charge.

Easy, Normal and Hard modes change the starting supplies and crew consumption. A co-op mode lets several players run the same base. At the end, a debrief explains what went right or wrong and shows the NASA facts behind it.

Benefits and intended impact
Players learn why real missions need shelters, power storage, closed-loop life support and local resources. They learn it by making trade-offs, not by reading. The goal is to make space science approachable for students and non-specialists. The game uses real NASA material:

  • the day-9 flare takes its class and date from the NASA DONKI space-weather database;
  • the flare window shows real ISS radiation measurements from NASA RadLab (OSDR);
  • the results screen has facts from the NASA OSDR archive on how weightlessness affects bones and muscles;
  • the daily oxygen, water and food needs are based on NASA’s published per-person figures (ECLSS);
  • the ice-scouting study cites the VIPER mission and lunar dust research.

A “NASA data” screen lists every source, and the game says plainly that its numbers are simplified.

Tools and technology

  • Languages and frameworks: TypeScript 7, React 19, Vite, Node.js 22.
  • Game core: a pure, deterministic game engine with no React, DOM or i18n code. An architecture check script enforces this boundary in CI.
  • Co-op: a lightweight Node server using Server-Sent Events. Because the engine is deterministic, all players see the same state.
  • Audio: procedural Web Audio API sound with no audio files (Apollo-style quindar tones, flare sirens, construction sounds, station ambience).
  • Quality: Vitest tests, an oxlint config, and a GitHub Actions CI pipeline.
  • Languages: Ukrainian (default), English and Russian.
  • Hardware: only a regular PC and a browser, with no special hardware.

How it is creative

  • It turns real NASA space-weather and radiation data into game events, so the mission is partly real history.
  • The audio is generated entirely in code, with no recorded assets.
  • Crew members have names and roles, and the debrief explains each outcome through a real NASA fact.
  • The shared, deterministic engine makes co-op possible with a very small server.
  • The map is hand-drawn art with an isometric build grid, with explicit rules for where building is allowed or forbidden.

Factors the team considered

  • Accuracy against playability: the numbers are simplified on purpose, but the principles are real, and the game says so.
  • Accessibility for the audience: three languages, short tasks with a stated reason, and difficulty modes.
  • Reliability: a pure engine that can be tested, with CI checks and architecture rules, so features from several teammates can be merged safely.
  • Performance and size: no external audio files, and the map is a vector SVG.
  • Fair multiplayer: deterministic simulation so players never diverge.
  • Honest use of data: every NASA source is credited inside the game.

Merge fix

The conflict happened because main had moved files (src/ui to src/features, map.ts to src/content/). Your old branch was based on the old layout. I resolved it, and on the result tsc, the architecture check and the unit tests pass.

I haven’t tried applying the patch on a clean checkout of main, and I haven’t built or played the result in a browser, so check the menu in the game yourself. The simplest way to apply it:

  1. git fetch then git checkout -b menu-and-cells origin/main
  2. git apply --index menu-and-cells.patch (the file is attached with this reply)
  3. git commit -m "Build-zone cells and new main menu" then git push -u origin menu-and-cells

Since main is the base, there will be no conflicts. The patch adds the menu background as src/assets/menu_bd.png, the file name already in your repo. The backdrop in src/styles/base.css now points to it.
